summary.en: Risings against Ottoman rule broke out across the Peloponnese and Central Greece in the spring of 1821. The 25th of March, Old Style, is the date the Greek state later chose to commemorate, though the first actions came earlier and in several places at once, including Alexandros Ypsilantis crossing the Pruth into Moldavia in February.

Greek forces took the Ottoman administrative capital of the Morea after a long siege. The capture was followed by the massacre of much of the Muslim and Jewish population of the town. It secured the Peloponnese for the revolution and set a pattern of reprisal that ran through the war on both sides.

Ottoman forces landed on Chios in response to a rising encouraged from Samos, and destroyed the island's population by killing, enslavement and flight. The scale of it turned European opinion toward the Greek cause, most visibly through Delacroix's painting of 1824.

title.en: The Death of Byron at Messolonghi

summary.en: Lord Byron, the most famous foreign supporter of the Greek cause, died of fever at Messolonghi three months after arriving to take a command. His death made the war a cause across Europe.

After a year under siege by Ottoman and Egyptian forces, the garrison and civilian population of Messolonghi attempted a mass breakout by night. Most were killed or taken. The town had already become the symbol of the revolution abroad, where Byron had died two years earlier, and its fall did more for Greek diplomacy than its defence had done for Greek arms.

A combined British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet in Navarino Bay. The engagement was not intended as a battle and no power had declared war. It nonetheless ended Ottoman capacity to hold the Peloponnese by sea and made Greek independence a question of terms rather than of outcome.
The first head of state of independent Greece was shot outside a church in Nafplio by members of the Mavromichalis clan. The disorder that followed convinced the Powers to impose a monarchy.

The Ottoman Empire recognised an independent Greek kingdom and accepted a frontier running from the Gulf of Arta to the Pagasetic Gulf. This was a more generous line than the London Protocol of 1830 had drawn. The new state held the Peloponnese, Attica, Central Greece, Euboea and the Cyclades, and roughly a third of the Greek speaking population of the region lived inside it.

The seventeen-year-old Bavarian prince chosen by the Powers as King of Greece arrived at Nafplio aboard a British frigate, with a regency and a loan. The monarchy that would rule Greece until 1974 began here.

title.en: The Union of the Ionian Islands

summary.en: Britain ceded the United States of the Ionian Islands to Greece, a protectorate it had held since 1815. The transfer was tied to the accession of George I and was the first enlargement of the kingdom. It was also the only one achieved by diplomacy alone, without a war.

title.en: The Cession of Thessaly and Arta

summary.en: Following the Congress of Berlin, the Ottoman Empire ceded Thessaly and the district of Arta to Greece without a war. Greece had mobilised but had not fought. The settlement left Elassona on the Ottoman side of the new line, where it stayed until 1912.

The settlement of the Second Balkan War divided Ottoman Macedonia between Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria. Greece gained Epirus, most of Macedonia including Thessaloniki, and the northern Aegean islands. In two campaigns the kingdom had roughly doubled in both territory and population, and had absorbed a population that was not predominantly Greek speaking.

title.en: The Treaty of Lausanne and the Exchange of Populations

summary.en: After the collapse of the Greek campaign in Asia Minor, Lausanne fixed the frontier with the new Turkish republic and provided for a compulsory exchange of populations on religious criteria. Roughly 1.2 million Orthodox Christians moved to Greece and around 400,000 Muslims moved the other way. It ended the Greek presence in Anatolia and reshaped the demography of Macedonia and Thrace within a few years.

title.en: The Italian Invasion and the Albanian Front

summary.en: Italy delivered an ultimatum in the small hours of 28 October 1940 and invaded from Albania three hours later. Metaxas rejected it. Within six weeks the Greek army had thrown the Italians back and was fighting inside Albania.

title.en: The Axis Invasion and the Triple Occupation

summary.en: German forces invaded on 6 April 1941 after the Italian attack from Albania had failed. Athens fell on 27 April and Crete followed in May. The country was then divided into German, Italian and Bulgarian zones of occupation while the Greek state continued to exist in exile, which is why the map shows occupation as a layer over sovereignty rather than in place of it.

The Paris Peace Treaty transferred the Dodecanese from Italy, which had held the islands since 1912, to Greece. Greek administration began in March 1947 and the formal union followed on 7 March 1948. It was the last enlargement of the Greek state.
